oneLineAnswer: Beclomethasone is a steroid medicine breathed in or sprayed in your nose to calm swelling and prevent symptoms.
whatItIs: Beclomethasone is a man-made steroid medicine. Specifically it is a corticosteroid, the family of hormones and drugs that calm inflammation. Your body makes its own corticosteroids too. The medicine is usually supplied as beclomethasone dipropionate. That form is a prodrug, meaning the body must convert it before it can act. Enzymes called esterases quickly split part of the molecule away. What remains is beclomethasone-17-monopropionate, the active compound. The FDA classifies beclomethasone as a corticosteroid that works as a corticosteroid hormone receptor agonist. In plain terms, it switches on the receptor that corticosteroids act through. It reaches you as an asthma inhaler, as a nasal spray, and inside some combination inhalers.
whatItDoes: Beclomethasone calms inflammation, the swelling and irritation inside airways and nasal passages.
As an inhaler it is approved to prevent asthma symptoms, not to relieve an attack already underway.
As a nasal spray it is approved to ease nasal symptoms of seasonal and perennial allergic rhinitis.
Seasonal allergic rhinitis is hay fever that follows pollen seasons. Perennial means symptoms last all year.
The label says the precise way corticosteroids improve asthma is not known.
It lists several anti-inflammatory effects, including blocking inflammatory cells and the mediators they release.
The inhaler label says symptoms can improve within a day, and full benefit can take three to four weeks.
howPeopleUseIt: People use the inhaler as a daily controller medicine to keep asthma quiet over time.
People use the nasal spray for congestion, sneezing and a runny nose caused by allergies.
Both come as metered-dose devices that release one measured puff at a time.
The inhaler is breath-actuated, so your own breath sets off each puff.
The nasal spray does not need priming, and neither does the inhaler used here.
One available inhaler combines beclomethasone with formoterol and glycopyrrolate.
Inhaler labels tell people to rinse the mouth with water without swallowing after inhaling.
That rinse is meant to lower the chance of a yeast infection in the mouth and throat.
Researchers have also studied the nasal spray in people with seasonal allergic rhinitis.

commonSideEffects: In inhaler trials, the most common side effects were oral thrush, upper respiratory infection, nasopharyngitis, throat pain and sinusitis.
Oral thrush is a yeast infection of the mouth and throat, caused by Candida albicans.
In nasal spray trials in people aged 12 and up, the most common effects were nasal discomfort, nosebleeds and headache.
In children aged 4 to 11 using the nasal spray, headache, fever, upper respiratory infection and nasopharyngitis were most common.
In a 52-week nasal spray trial, nosebleeds occurred in 45 of 415 people on the medicine. Only 2 of 111 people on placebo had them.
Back pain, headache, nausea and cough were also reported at lower rates with the inhaler.
seriousSigns: Rarely, a puff can set off bronchospasm, a sudden narrowing of the airways with more wheezing. The label calls this potentially life-threatening.
High doses, or long use, can cause hypercorticism and adrenal suppression. That means the body's own cortisol system is damped down.
The label warns that adrenal insufficiency has caused deaths when people moved from systemic steroids to an inhaler.
The label says people moving from oral corticosteroids to an inhaler need slow tapering. Adrenal function takes months to recover.
Chickenpox and measles can run a more serious or fatal course in people taking corticosteroids.
Existing tuberculosis, fungal, bacterial, viral or parasitic infections can worsen, as can eye infections from herpes simplex.
Corticosteroids may slow growth speed in children. The label says growth should be measured routinely.
Reduced bone mineral density has been seen with long-term inhaled corticosteroids.
Glaucoma, raised eye pressure, blurred vision and cataracts have been reported with long-term use.
Serious allergic reactions have been reported, including anaphylaxis, angioedema, hives, rash and bronchospasm.
Nasal spray reports include more frequent and sometimes more severe nosebleeds, plus nasal erosions and nasal ulceration.
Nasal septal perforation, a hole in the wall between the nostrils, has been reported.
Postmarketing reports for inhaled corticosteroids include aggression, depression, sleep problems, hyperactivity and suicidal thoughts, mostly in children.
Blurred vision and central serous chorioretinopathy, a fluid leak under the retina, are also listed.
Fewer than 2 percent of people stopped the nasal spray trials because of side effects.
whoShouldAvoid: Anyone allergic to beclomethasone dipropionate or another ingredient in the product should not use it.
The inhaler is not meant for status asthmaticus, a severe asthma attack that needs intensive care.
The nasal spray label says to avoid it after recent nasal ulcers, nasal surgery or nasal trauma, until healing.
The label advises caution if you have active or inactive tuberculosis of the respiratory tract.
The same caution applies to untreated fungal, bacterial, parasitic or viral infections, and to ocular herpes simplex.
Neither form is established for children under 4 years old.

interactions: The nasal aerosol label states that no drug interaction studies have been performed with that product.
The inhaler label used here has no separate drug interaction section.
The labels warn that immune suppression can worsen infections, rather than listing specific interacting medicines.
The inhaler label says some beclomethasone is absorbed into the bloodstream. At higher doses it can act throughout the body, so other steroid exposure matters.
pregnancyAndChildren: Beclomethasone has not been tested in adequate, well-controlled studies of pregnant women. The labels say no published study, including large birth registries, has linked these steroids to more birth defects. Human data therefore cannot confirm or rule out a risk to a fetus. In the United States general population, the background chance of a major birth defect is about 2 to 4 percent. The chance of miscarriage is about 15 to 20 percent. Poorly controlled asthma in pregnancy is itself linked to preeclampsia, premature birth, low birth weight and small-for-gestational-age babies. The labels say asthma control in pregnancy should be watched closely. Whether beclomethasone passes into human milk is not known. Other corticosteroids have been found in milk. Both the inhaler and the nasal spray are approved from age 4. Below that age, safety and effectiveness have not been established. One 12-month study followed children aged 5 to 11. Growth was about 0.5 cm per year slower on an HFA beclomethasone inhaler than on a CFC beclomethasone inhaler. The label notes the comparison product was used with a large-volume spacer.
whatWeDoNotKnow: Whether beclomethasone passes into human milk is unknown, as is any effect on a breastfed baby.
How much the small growth slowdown in children affects final adult height is unknown.
Whether children catch up on growth after stopping treatment has not been adequately studied.
The label says the meaning of small bone density changes for long-term fracture risk is unknown.
It is not fully understood how corticosteroids actually improve asthma.
The clinical importance of beclomethasone's receptor binding compared with other steroids is unknown.
The inhaler trials enrolled too few people aged 65 and over to show whether they respond differently.
The nasal aerosol label reports no drug interaction studies for that product.
No LiverTox entry specific to beclomethasone was found during this review.
Nothing in this record states a dose or a personal plan for using beclomethasone. That was deliberate.

gaps: NCCIH has no beclomethasone page: https://www.nccih.nih.gov/health/beclomethasone returns HTTP 404, so no NCCIH content appears here.

MedlinePlus drug monographs were excluded deliberately because NLM states they are American Society of Health-System Pharmacists content. MedlinePlus use here is limited to its public domain health topic pages.
An openFDA query using the British spelling Beclometasone returned HTTP 404. The spelling Beclomethasone returned labels.
https://medlineplus.gov/allergicrhinitis.html returned HTTP 404 and could not be used.
LiverTox was checked and no beclomethasone entry was found, so no liver injury detail is included.

The openFDA and DailyMed labels are separate publishers but both carry FDA-authored label text, so they are not fully independent of each other. PubChem, ClinicalTrials.gov and MedlinePlus are independent of the label text.
Examine.com, Labdoor, MSKCC About Herbs, ConsumerLab, WebMD, Healthline, Drugs.com and RxList were excluded because they are copyrighted and forbid reproduction.
Side effect rates come from controlled trials only. Both labels warn those rates may not match everyday practice.
No fetched source quantifies how much beclomethasone raises the risk of eye problems or bone density loss.
Dose amounts, how to take beclomethasone, and any personal plan were left out on purpose and are not a sourcing gap.
summary: This record covers beclomethasone's identity, approved uses, side effects, safety warnings, and remaining gaps.
